paper.title: Analysis of Search Heuristics in the Multi-Armed Bandit Setting

unmapped: Deterministic query: any query set containing the winner i* returns i*; goal is to identify i*
settings.definition_quote: Given $k,n \in \natnum$ and a winner $i^* \in [1..n]$. An algorithm can perform a query on a chosen $A \subseteq [1..n]$ with $|A|\leq k$ deterministically returning some element $q(A) \in A$. We assume that, for all $A~\subseteq~[1..n]$ with $|A| \leq k$ and $i^* \in A$, we have $q(A) = i^*$.

unmapped: Performance measured via stationary distribution / hitting time of a search heuristic's Markov chain rather than regret or fixed-confidence sample complexity
settings.definition_quote: Given $n \in \natnum$ and a matrix $M$ with values in $(0,1)$ such that, for all $1 \leq i < j \leq n$, we have $M(i,j) + M(j,i) = 1$ and $M(i,i)=1$. An algorithm can perform a query on any two different arms $i,j \in \firstInts{n}$ with return value $i$ with probability~$M(i,j)$ and with return value $j$ otherwise. The goal is to identify $i^*\in \firstInts{n}$ such that, for all $i \in \firstInts{n} \setminus \{i^*\},$ $M(i^*,i) > 0.5$.

settings.name_in_paper: Plackett-Luce model, comparison of two arms
unmapped: Number of duels x is fixed in advance (non-adaptive majority vote)
settings.definition_quote: Assume we have an underlying utility $u_i \in \mathbb{R}$ for each arm $i \in \firstInts{n}$. Then the probability that arm $i \in \firstInts{n}$ wins in a subset of competitors $S \subset \firstInts{n}$ is defined as $\Prob{i | S} = \frac{u_i}{\sum_{j \in S} u_j}$.

algorithms.name: Majority vote over x duels (boosted query)

source.quote: The Round-Robin algorithm identifies a winner within $n-1$ queries of size~$2$.

results.notes: Paper's n is the number of arms K. Deterministic feedback, so the bound holds surely.

source.quote: The Random Search algorithm performs queries of size $2$ and maintains the winner as $i^*$ after an expected number of $n$ iterations. The distribution of the number of iterations until maintaining the winner as $i^*$ follows $\mathrm{Geo}(1/n)$.

results.notes: The number of iterations is Geo(1/n); the expectation is n. The algorithm never stops, so this is the expected time until the winner is first held, not a stopping time.

symbols.p_l: bound such that M(i*, i) >= 1 - p_l > 1/2 for all i != i*
symbols.p_u: bound such that M(i*, i) <= 1 - p_u < 1 for all i != i*

source.label: lem:oneonEA_stochasticQueries
source.quote: Suppose that there are bounds $p_l,p_u$ such that, for all $i \in S$ with $i \neq i^*$, $1 > 1-p_u \geq M(i^*, i) \geq 1- p_l > \frac{1}{2}.$ Then the stationary distribution can be bounded by $\pi_{i^*} \geq \frac{1-p_l}{1-p_l+(n-1)\cdot p_l} > \frac{1-p_l}{1-p_l+n\cdot p_l}$ and $\pi_{i^*} \leq \frac{1-p_u}{1-p_u+(n-1)\cdot p_u} < \frac{1-p_u}{n\cdot p_u}$.

results.notes: This is a statement about the (1+1) EA, not a lower bound over algorithms. The record is a lower bound on the stationary probability of the Condorcet winner (higher is better). The lemma also gives the upper bound pi_{i*} <= (1-p_u)/(1-p_u+(n-1)p_u), which shows the EA's weakness. Proposition prop:bin:stationary_dist_bounds and Corollary cor:oneoneEA_Stationary are special cases of this lemma: with p = Theta(1/n^2), pi = 1 - Theta(1/n).

symbols.eps_mix: total-variation accuracy defining the mixing time tau(eps)

source.label: lem:oneoneEA_mixingTime
source.quote: Consider the \oneoneEA variant for the Condorcet winner search and $n \in \N$. Let $i^*_t\in S$ be the underlying Markov chain ... Then, $\tau(\epsilon) \leq n \ln (1/\epsilon).$

results.notes: Mixing time of the Markov chain induced by the algorithm; the quantity is a number of iterations, not regret. The probability label is a placeholder: the bound is deterministic and is on a total-variation mixing time.

symbols.p_l: bound such that M(i*, i) >= 1 - p_l > 1/2 for all i != i*
symbols.eps_mix: accuracy in the mixing time tau(eps) used in Sudholt's theorem

source.label: cor_exp_opt_time
source.quote: For all $i \in S$ with $i \neq i^*$, let $M(i^*, i) \geq 1-p_l > \frac{1}{2}$. Then, the expected optimization time is at most $\tau(\epsilon) \cdot \BigO{\log(1/\pi_{i^*})}/\pi_{i^*} = n \cdot \ln \left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)\cdot \BigO{\log \left({1+\frac{(n-1)p_l}{1-p_l}}\right)\cdot \left(1+\frac{(n-1)p_l}{1-p_l}\right)}$.

results.notes: Expected optimisation time: the expected number of iterations (one duel each) until the Condorcet winner is the incumbent, obtained from Sudholt's theorem. In the paper the O(·) wraps only the log and product factor; the n ln(1/eps) factor is outside it. Part (2), with p = o(1)/n, gives (1+o(1)) n ln(1/eps) O(log(1+o(1))) and is not recorded separately.

symbols.u_i: Plackett-Luce utility of the better arm i
symbols.u_j: Plackett-Luce utility of the worse arm j

tuning: delta (paper's epsilon) is the target failure probability

source.label: Thm:NecessaryNumberDuelsTwoArms
source.quote: Assume two arms $i,j \in \firstInts{n}$ with the underlying Plackett-Luce Model and $u_i > u_j$. ... Let the winning probability of arm $i$ fulfill $\frac{u_i}{u_i+u_j}>\frac{x+1}{2x}$. Then arm $i$ wins in expectation more often against arm $j$ with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ if the number of duels $x$ between $i$ and $j$ is greater than $x \geq \frac{2(u_i+u_j)^2}{(u_j-u_i)^2} \ln\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right).$

results.notes: Number of duels sufficient for the majority vote to pick the better arm with probability at least 1-epsilon (Hoeffding). The paper's epsilon is the failure probability delta. The side condition involves x itself.

symbols.tau_min: lower bound on pheromone values (algorithm parameter)
symbols.p: M(i*,i) >= 1-p for all i != i*, with p in [0,1/4]

source.quote: Let $n \in \natnum$, $\taumin,\rho \in (0,1/n)$ with $\taumin \leq 1/(10n)$. ... Suppose there is $p \in [0,1/4]$ such that $\forall i \in S \setminus \{i^*\}: M(i^*,i) \geq 1-p.$ Then it takes the algorithm an expected time of $\BigO{\frac{1}{\taumin\rho} + \frac{\log(1/p)}{\rho}}$ until reaching a marginal probability of at least $1-3p-n\taumin$ for the Condorcet winner for the first time.

results.notes: Expected number of iterations (one duel each) until the Condorcet winner's marginal probability first reaches at least 1-3p-n*tau_min. The quantity is a hitting time, so it is recorded as other. The proof relies on drift theorems and only sketches a restart argument.
